checks: Matched 7ff8cebaefda7361 §7 and checked its source digest. The frozen claim uses ordinary raw closed-halfspace depth in dimension one and needs no previous theorem.

On the line the infimum reduces to the two closed through-point rays. Outside [0,1] a containing ray misses both the interval and the atom. With the atom at g both rays count its full mass, whereas one ray misses the atom and has mass below 1/2 at every other point of the interval. The maximizing point is uniquely g.

For the moving atom, 0<t<1/4 ensures g<a_t<1. Below a_t in [0,1], the two masses sum to 1+t. Their minimum reaches their mean only where they agree, y=(1+t)/2. The inequality t/2<sqrt(t) puts this point strictly below the atom. At and above the atom the closed right ray has mass at most 1−a_t+t, strictly below (1+t)/2 by the same inequality, including the atom counted on the boundary.

The common unperturbed maximum is 1/2, so the exact formulas give slopes 1 and 1/2. Both laws converge to the point mass at g, which charges both canonical boundaries. The example establishes insufficiency of the weak limit alone in that case.
